Sorry if this is a repost. My first try appears to have been swallowed by the goat.
Why does HalfLife2 update itself so often?

Those are usually tiny changes you won't even notice. Rare bug fixes, etc. Since steam doesn't support delta coding, if a file changes, you have to download the whole new file. A 21MB download could very well be a 50 byte change.
How come Steam doesn't support delta coding? Wouldn't it be great if it did? At least on the bandwidth consumption side.
I have no Idea why they don't implement it. At least you only have to download the files that changed.

Steam does support delta patching and has for a while. Since at least 2012. Not all games support it as there was a conversion process required when games switched to the new system, but I distinctly remember TF2 going through a Steam-pipe update that converted it to the new delta-friendly format.

EDIT: Found a source.
This was really a big issue with The Witcher 2. The main file was 8 GB if I remember right and a minor change would require you to download the entire file. They fixed that a few years ago.

Half Life 2 uses Valve's Source Engine for its underlying framework. This same engine is used in many of their First Person Shooters, including Counter Strike: Global Offense, which is heavily played, with some level of professional gaming as well.As it has a professional scene, it must stay as up to date as possible from bugs.

But any time there is an update to the Source Engine itself, all games that use it must install the same update. While that update might simply be to help avoid Out-Of-Bounds maneuvers in CS:GO through the engine itself, Half Life 2 gets it as well, because it uses that engine.

At least, that is how I understand the system. I could be off in a few details.

Hello all,

I've been playing with SPI on an atmega and have a raspberry pi master successfully communicating with the atmega slave. It currently very rudimentary. Just talking a single byte at a time. I had to slow the speed down a lot for the slave to have time to reply, but that shouldn't be an issue.

Now I'm faced with a challenge that I have no experience with. I'd like to be able to transfer much more data (like RTC date time, ADC values, etc). I guess I'm looking for a protocol with addressing and allows for replies of multiple bytes. It will need to be simple enough so that the atmega can reply quickly.

I'm sure this has been done plenty of times before. Any suggestions or advice would be very appreciated!
SPI with Atmega. Looking for a simple and reliable data protocol. Suggestions?

Update:

I found some decent example code in this AVR freaks thread. I've also seen reference to the Modbus protocol being adapted to SPI. Modbus includes addressing, functions (read/write, etc), 16-bit registers, dynamic length packets, and a CRC16 checksum. So that sounds promising.

I'm still researching, but my solution will probably be based on these.
